title: A clinical decision support system to predict the efficacy for EGFR-TKIs based on artificial neural network
author: Xiao Liang; Runwei Guan; Jiamin Zhu; Yue Meng; Jing Zhu; Yuxiang Yang; Yanan Cui; Jiali Dai; Weidong Mao; Liting Lv; Dong Shen; Renhua Guo
text:
Abstract
Background
The efficacy of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) was affected by numerous factors. In the study, we developed and validated an artificial neural network (ANN) system based on clinical characteristics and next-generation sequencing (NGS) to support clinical decisions.
Methods
A multicenter retrospective non-interventional study was conducted. 240 patients from three hospitals with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and EGFR mutation were tested by NGS before the first treatment. All patients received formal EGFR-TKIs treatment. Five different models were individually trained to predict the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs based on one medical center with 188 patients. Two independent cohorts from other medical centers were collected for external validation.
Results
Compared with logistic regression, four machine learning methods showed better predicting abilities for EGFR-TKIs. The inclusion of NGS tests improved the predictive power of models. ANN performed best on the dataset with mutations TP53, RB1, PIK3CA, EGFR mutation sites, and tumor mutation burden (TMB). The prediction accuracy, recall and AUC were 0.82, 0.82, and 0.82, respectively in our final model. In the external validation set, ANN still showed good performance and differentiated patients with poor outcomes. Finally, a clinical decision support software based on ANN was developed and provided a visualization interface for clinicians.
Conclusion
This study provides an approach to assess the efficacy of NSCLC patients with first-line EGFR-TKI treatment. Software is developed to support clinical decisions.

Keywords: NSCLC, EGFR-TKIs, NGS, ANN, TP53, TMB
Introduction
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality with an estimated 1.8 million deaths in 2020, which imposes a substantial public health burden around the world (Siegel et al. 2021; Sung 2020). Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer with high invasion, dismal survival rates, and limited therapeutic options (Rodriguez-Canales et al. 2016). The Iressa Pan-Asia Study (IPASS) in 2009 marked a watershed for the therapy of NSCLC (Mok et al. 2009). Before the IPASS study, patients with advanced NSCLC received unselected chemotherapy, in which the 1-year survival rate of advanced lung cancer patients with chemotherapy was low (Scagliotti et al. 2008). Only 35–40% of these patients were alive at 1 year. IPASS study laid the foundation for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) as a standard first-line regimen for the treatment of advanced lung cancer patients with EGFR mutation. EGFR-TKIs have extended the survival of NSCLC (Mok et al. 2009).
Drug resistance greatly limits the usefulness of EGFR-TKIs (Lin et al. 2014). Although the response rate of EGFR-TKIs as first-line treatment was even up to 70% and the progression-free survival (PFS) was around 10 months (Inoue 2020), EGFR-TKIs are still less effective or even ineffective for some patients. EGFR-TKIs combined with chemotherapies or anti-angiogenic therapies have been proven to prolong the PFS and increase toxicity in some patients (Saito et al. 2019; Noronha et al. 2020). The PFS in some studies has also translated into an increased overall survival (OS) (Noronha et al. 2020). With this comes a cost in increased adverse drug reactions and hospital stays (Noronha et al. 2020). Screening ineffective patients and bringing earlier interventions display great clinical implications.
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is widely available, revealing the high heterogeneity of lung cancer at a molecular level (Nguyen, et al. 2022). With massive sequencing, more resistance mutations in EGFR-mutated patients were discovered. Many mutations have been proven to be associated with the poor efficacy of EGFR-TKIs (Guo et al. 2020; Liang 2022). Recently, deep learning (DL) has also been widely used in different fields of medicine. Models based on DL have been demonstrated to predict the prognosis and risks of various diseases (Li et al. 2021). At the present stage, there are some excellent predictive models to identify the efficacy of drugs (Song et al. 2020; Peng et al. 2019). Most of these models are based on radionics methods. It increases the difficulty of clinical translation. Herein, we first attempt to develop and validate a clinical decision support system for predicting the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs based on machine learning and NGS.
Methods
Eligibility criteria of patients and study design
A total of 240 patients were enrolled in this study. 188 patients were from the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University and underwent first-line EGFR-TKIs treatment between December 2014 and August 2021 as cohort 1. An independent cohort with 52 patients was from Jiangyin people’s hospital and Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University as external validation (cohort2). All patients underwent NGS tests. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of these three hospitals.
A detailed study design is shown in Fig. 1A. We assumed that the data in the training set and test set were independently identically distributed, therefore, to make the data randomization and robust, the data were shuffled. Then the data were divided into two parts in cohort1, 70% for the training set and 30% for the test set. Besides, the ten-fold cross-validation was used to evaluate the generalization of the model.
Five different models were trained to distinguish the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs treatment including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), XGBoost, and artificial neural network (ANN). The main hyperparameters of machine learning models after fine-tuning are shown in Table S1–S3.
Under normal circumstances, we think that the generalization of traditional machine learning methods is relatively weak, and the solution to nonlinear discrimination problems is weaker than deep learning. Therefore, we also try to use ANN to predict efficacy. We designed a nano-ANN similar to a multilayer perceptron, which is shown in Fig. 1B. The input layer is various discrete data of the patient with a bias value. The hidden layer includes a layer of batch normalization, three layers of neurons with bias and the dropout, two layers of the ReLU activation function, and a layer of the sigmoid activation function. The output layer is two discrete floating-point numbers, used to represent the category results. The cross-entropy function is used to calculate the loss value of the artificial neural network for gradient descent and backpropagation. The formula of the cross entropy function was shown below.
In addition, we use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter 2018) as the gradient descent optimizer to backpropagate the artificial neural network. The hyperparameters of AdamW are shown in Table S4.
Metrics and evaluation
Clinical data included sex, age at diagnosis, smoking status, size of tumors, metastatic burden, and treatment regimens. PFS, which was defined as survival time from the beginning of first-line EGFR-TKIs to disease progression or death was used to assess the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs. Efficacy evaluation indicators of EGFR-TKIs included poor efficacy and good efficacy. The cut-off value of PFS was 12 months. The cut-off of TMB is five mutations/Mb (Offin et al. 2019). The cut-off age is 65. Metastatic burdens of patients were described as low (number of metastatic sites < 2), intermediate (number of metastatic sites = 2), and high (number of metastatic sites > 2). EGFR mutation sites fall into three subgroups: exon 19, exon 21, and others. The NGS test is a mature customized detection method used in many earlier studies (Liang 2022; Cui et al. 2022).
Univariate analyses were performed to screen for factors to be evaluated in the LR. Factors associated with efficacy with a univariate p value < 0.1 were included in the LR. In the models, the confusion matrix is the basis for the metrics and evaluation. The confusion matrix is shown in Fig. 1C. Based on the confusion matrix, two metrics, accuracy, and recall, were used to evaluate the performance of different models. Detailed definitions were below.
In addition, to evaluate the confidence of the model, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and area under curve (AUC) were considered to measure the model in another dimension. For ROC, different thresholds will cause the probability of predicting true positives and false positives to change, and ROC will traverse all thresholds to find the point that makes the highest true positives and the lowest false positives. The area under the ROC curve, we call it AUC, represents the probability that any pair of samples (positive and negative) is taken, and the score of the positive sample is greater than the score of the negative sample.
Statistical analysis
Kaplan–Meier survival curves and log-rank tests were used to compare prognosis differences. COX regression model was used to evaluate the Hazard ratios (HRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). SPSS 23 was used for statistical analysis. R 4.0.2 and GraphPad Prism 7.0 were used to generate plots. Python 3.7 was used to build deep learning models. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Result
Clinical characteristics
One hundred eighty-eight patients from the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University were included in cohort 1 for model construction and internal validation. 80% of patients were included as a training set randomly and others were applied as an internal validation set in cohort 1. All patients were treated with first-line EGFR-TKIs.
Logistic regression and DL
For predicting the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs and screening the insensitive populations, five different models based on clinical characteristics (Dataset 1) were individually trained. For LR, the accuracy and recall were 61 and 68, respectively (Fig. 2A and B). The accuracies of SVM, RF, XGBoost, and ANN were 0.65, 0.71, 0.68, and 0.65, respectively (Fig. 2A). The recall of four models were 0.74, 0.78, 0.74, and 0.74, respectively (Fig. 2B). SVM, RF and XGBoost, and ANN worked better to identify the efficacy for EGFR-TKIs than LR. However, the AUC of these models was not unsatisfactory (Fig. 2C).
Model optimization based on NGS
Prediction models based on clinical characteristics were unsatisfactory. Genetic mutations could result in the resistance of EGFR-TKIs (Guo et al. 2020). Taking into account the stability and universality of the model, the top 10 frequencies of mutations in NGS tests of our cohort (TP53, RB1, PIK3CA, CTNMB1, RBM10, APC, LRP1B, ATM, SETD2, CDKN2A) were selected, as demonstrated in Fig. 3A. Hazard ratio (HR) of mutations were calculated for the covariate of treatment by Cox regression model and shown in the forest plot (Fig. 3B). TP53 was the most common mutation (118/188, 62.8%) (Fig. 3A) in our cohort and had a close relationship with poor efficacy (HR = 1.963, 95% CI 1.38–2.856, P < 0.001) (Fig. 3B). Other high frequency and malignant potential mutations included RB1 (20/188, 10.6%) (Fig. 3A) and PIK3CA (18/188, 9.6%) (Fig. 3A). These three mutations were often reported to be associate with resistance to EGFR-TKIs in previous studies(Guo et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2020; Jin et al. 2018). Whether mutations per se or numbers of these three mutations could differentiate patients with poor outcomes (Fig. 3D and E). TMB was also related to outcomes of patients (Log-rank P = 0.002) (Fig. 3C). So TP53, RB1, PIK3CA, TMB, and EGFR mutation sites were included in our model. Clinical characteristics combined with the mutated situation and the number of mutated genes were included in Dataset 2 and Dataset 3. Compared with Dataset1, the predictability of models was increased in Dataset2 and Dataset3 (Fig. 4A–C). AUC was substantially increased in every model with NGS tests. ANN had the highest ACC, recall, and AUC among other models in Dataset 2. The convergence and ROC curves of ANN in tenfold-cross validation were in Fig. 4D and E.
External validation
An external data set (cohort2) was used to validate these models. The ACC, recall, and AUC were 0.83, 0.89, and 0.81. ANN model still showed good performance. In the ANN model, PFS and overall survival (OS) of patients with good efficacy differed significantly from those with poor efficacy (P = 0.044) (Fig. 5A and B).
Clinical decision support system and visualization
To improve the efficiency of medical staff, a clinical diagnosis decision-making client based on Python GUI was developed, as shown in Fig. 6A. The system uses an artificial neural network model to run in the back end, and the artificial neural network model will provide corresponding treatment recommendations based on the model discrimination results. The prediction procedure is shown in Fig. 6B. Under the prediction procedure, a clinical decision support system can recommend treatment for patients.
Discussion
The response rate to first-line EGFR-TKIs approaches 70%, which is much higher than chemotherapy. However, it still means that almost 30% of patients cannot benefit from EGFR-TKIs. It has clinical implications to predict the efficacy and screening the less effective patients. There are still many challenges to developing a practical clinical tool for assessing the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs. Therapeutic resistance is a complex and multi-factorial participating process. At the present stage, models based on imaging have demonstrated the ability to predict the efficacy of cancer treatment (Chetan and Gleeson 2021). These models often lack generalization and are difficult to transduce. Thus, we attempted to develop models based on clinical characteristics, genotypes and artificial intelligence.
Many clinical characteristics are known to predict the efficacy for EGFR-TKIs. Larger tumors are always thought to be associated with poor prognosis (Pan et al. 2019). Patients with concomitant brain metastases and pleural metastasis are also reported to have bad outcomes (Chen et al. 2019). Identifying the efficacy for EGFR-TKIs is challenging. Our five models all showed inferior predictive performance (Fig. 2).
Co-mutations play an important role in the drug resistant of EGFR-TKIs (Tan et al. 2021). TP53 was the most frequent and impactful concurrent mutation in lung cancer with EGFR mutation. The co-mutation rate of TP53 ranged from 54.6 to 64.6% (Skoulidis and Heymach 2019). The co-mutation of TP53 influenced the natural history of patients with EGFR-mutant and allowed for the diversification of subclone. It prompted the therapeutic resistance. A large number of studies also identified that TP53 can be a negative prognostic marker for the outcomes following EGFR-TKIs (Canale et al. 2017; Labbe et al. 2017; Kim et al. 2019). As an important early genetic event of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, the inactivation of RB1 often harbors TP53 co-alterations and controls the cell cycle with mutation rate of approximately 10% (Skoulidis and Heymach 2019; Jordan et al. 2017). TP53 and RB1 co-mutations in EGFR-mutant LUAD also increase the risk of small-cell transformation (Niederst et al. 2015). ATM alterations, IDH1 mutations and PTEN mutations were also reported to be associated with shorter PFS and OS in patients receiving first-line EGFR-TKIs (Blons et al. 2021). LKB1/AMPK pathway was shown to reduce sensitivity of EGFR-TKIs in vitro (Cheng et al. 2021). After analyzing genomic changes, TP53, RB1, and PIK3CA were selected as important parameters in the final model. EGFR mutation sites and tumor mutation burden (TMB) are also reported to be strongly correlated with the therapeutic response of EGFR-TKIs (Offin et al. 2019; Hong et al. 2018). We integrated these genomic signatures which were demonstrated to increase the stability and accuracy of models. NGS tests also increase the accessibility of models. With the constantly mature technology and gradually decreasing costs of NGS tests, genotypes of most NSCLC patients can be definitive prior to first-line treatment. In conclusion, genotypes well assisted in predicting the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs.
In the last two decades, ML models have been widely applied in medical and health sciences (Cruz and Wishart 2007). It is evident that ML models have improved the understanding of cancer progression (Kourou et al. 2015). It is the first model to predict the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs based on ANN. ANN can handle classification problems satisfactorily and even serve as a gold standard in some tasks. Hidden layers represent the neural connections in the mathematical process (Fig. 1B). As is known to all, ANN has a stronger fitting ability for linearly indivisible data than traditional machine learning models, but at the same time, they also have higher requirements for the amount of data. Therefore, small sample learning is always a great challenge for deep learning. We study and explore a nano-level artificial neural network, which can quickly converge in our small-scale datasets, and achieve good generalization and accuracy in internal and external validation sets. Prior to clinical translation, ethical issues, and clinical interpretability should be taken into further account.
The risk of progression with different generation EGFR-TKIs is an important research direction. The efficacy of first-line osimertinib is much better than previous EGFR-TKIs (Soria et al. 2018). In the FLAURA study, the median PFS of osimertinib was up to 18.9 months, which was prominently longer than gefitinib or erlotinib. Given the excellent efficacy of osimertinib, the number of untreated patients with osimertinib who meet enrollment criteria is limited. We decided to exclude patients with osimertinib from our model. With the large-scale use of Osimertinib in untreated EGFR-mutated NSCLC, the comparison between first-generation EGFR-TKIs or second-generation EGFR-TKIs and third-generation EGFR-TKIs will also be included in the next improved model after completing the follow-up. Further work will be dedicated to addressing the selection of more specific individualized treatment including the combinations with anti-angiogenic therapies or chemotherapies and the difference between first-generation EGFR-TKIs or second-generation EGFR-TKIs and third-generation EGFR-TKIs.
There are still some limits to our study. Only first-generation EGFR-TKIs and second-generation EGFR-TKIs are involved in the model. Our new model needs validation for more third-generation EGFR-TKIs. The sample size should also be enlarged in the future to make the model more stable. Our model still requires more external validation sets to test its generalizability. Additionally, all patients in this study are from China, future studies are warranted to validate whether these findings are broadly applicable.
Conclusion
We describe a DL approach to distinguish the efficacy of patients with EGFR-TKI therapy and have completed initial clinical translation. The approach can work as a clinical decision support system of EGFR-TKI therapy.
